evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, 漢字「七」：字形演變
evidence.text: The entry identifies a bronze inscription and cites 集成04320, then proposes that 七 originally meant “cut,” that a short stroke was added across the horizontal stroke in bronze forms, and that the small-seal form bent the vertical stroke to distinguish it from 十. It says 七 was later borrowed for the numeral and 刀 was added to make 切. This is a source’s analysis, not a settled conclusion.
evidence.title: 漢字「七」：字形演變

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports that 七 has recorded the numeral from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms. It describes the early graph as crossed horizontal and vertical strokes, and says a bent lower vertical stroke appears after the Eastern Han. Its proposed explanation for the graphic change is avoidance of confusion with 十. The article cites specific examples, including oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 inscription 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Eastern Han-period Wuwei medical slips. It also discusses alternate spellings 桼、漆、柒 and copy or printing errors in those forms; these are numeral spellings, not necessarily stages in 七’s graphic development.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The database says interpretations of 七’s shape are numerous and unresolved. It favors the analysis that 七 is an early form of 切: 一 and 丨 represent cutting across a line, and after 七 was borrowed for the numeral, 刀 was added to form 切. It also records a different proposal that the shape originated in a hand gesture. This supports reporting the cut analysis as a proposal rather than established graphic fact.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi (as quoted in the CUHK character database and dossier)
evidence.text: The Shuowen explanation is 陽之正也。从一，微陰从中衺出也。凡七之屬皆从七. This is a Han-period cosmological interpretation of the graph; it does not independently establish the original graphic referent. The CUHK entry quotes it while noting competing interpretations.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Institute of History and Natural Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 詩經·豳風·七月
evidence.text: The transmitted poem repeatedly uses 七 in calendrical and counting contexts, including 七月流火 and 七月食瓜. This establishes an early textual numeral use, but the page does not date the physical witness or by itself establish when the poem was composed. It is lexical evidence for the numeral, separate from claims about the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 诗经·豳风·七月

evidence.source: Kotobank, entry citing 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通
evidence.field: Japanese lexical attestations and later senses
evidence.text: The dictionary gives a Manyōshū example (8th century, poem 4.743) for なな ‘seven’; 古事記 (712) for a use meaning that seven people perform an action; and 史記抄 (1477) as an example of the Sino-Japanese reading しち for the number seven. It also records a specialized later sense ‘gambler’ with a 1744 example. These are Japanese word and usage histories, not evidence for the origin of the Chinese graph.
evidence.title: 七(シチ)とは？ 意味や使い方

evidence.source: Oxford University Press, William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction system and scope
evidence.text: The book description identifies this as a reconstruction of Old Chinese phonology, morphology, and lexicon based on several kinds of comparative evidence. The locally supplied Baxter–Sagart row for 七 gives MC tshit and OC *[tsʰ]i[t], gloss ‘seven’ (local file `sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv`, 七 row). That local table row was checked as requested, but it is local data, not an independently inspected external character record. No 切 row was supplied, and the accessible external pages inspected here do not establish a matched reconstruction pair for 七 and 切; therefore sound similarity is not treated as proof that 七 originally named cutting.
evidence.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium, Unicode Standard Version 17.0 code chart
evidence.text: The official chart lists 七 at U+4E03. It verifies the character identity and code point, but the chart PDF could not be opened in this session due to a content-size fetch failure. The official character-specific Unihan record URL was also attempted and returned an internal fetch error, so no external claim about kMandarin is made from those pages. The local Unihan row supplied for 七 is `kMandarin=qī` in `sources/unihan/Unihan_Readings.txt`; this remains a local-row check, not a verified external Unihan page.

evidence.title: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, CJK Unified Ideographs code chart

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study identifies 七 as the long-standing graph for the numeral. It reports crossed horizontal and vertical strokes from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms, citing oracle-bone 合集10650 and Western Zhou bronze 小盂鼎 (集成2839). It describes later differentiation from 十, with a rightward bend in the lower vertical becoming established after the Eastern Han. This account treats the history as numeral writing and graphic differentiation; it does not establish an earlier ‘cut’ meaning.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, 漢字「七」：字形演變
evidence.text: The page proposes that 七 originally meant ‘cut,’ that bronze forms added a short stroke across the horizontal, and that the seal form bent the vertical to distinguish 七 from 十. It further says the numeral use was a loan and 刀 was added to make 切. These are the page’s assertions; they conflict with the Zhengzhou study’s account of 七 as numeral from oracle-bone writing onward, so the cut origin and borrowing sequence remain disputed.
evidence.title: 漢字「七」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The database favors an analysis of 七 as an early form of 切: 一 and 丨 are interpreted as a line cut across, after which 七 was borrowed for the numeral and 刀 added in 切. It also describes interpretations as numerous and unresolved and records an alternative hand-gesture proposal. The parsing of the strokes and their semantic role are thus part of a disputed account, not independently established component meanings.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study cites oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 bronze 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Wuwei medical slips from around the Eastern Han transition. It says the pre-Eastern-Han crossing form persisted until early Western Han clerical writing and that the lower vertical later bent right. These cited objects supply examples in a graphic sequence, but the web page does not provide a directly inspectable image of each example in this research pass.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

gaps: The meaning ‘cut’ for the earliest graph remains disputed: the inspected sources also describe alternative interpretations, and one scholarly numeral-use study treats 七 as the numeral from oracle-bone evidence onward. The early graph’s depicted referent and original spoken name are not independently established by the sources inspected.

No directly inspectable primary comparative entry for 切 was found to validate the proposed sound relationship with 七 within one reconstruction system. Do not infer 七’s proposed source-word pronunciation from 七’s reconstruction alone; the local Baxter–Sagart row supports only 七: MC tshit, OC *[tsʰ]i[t].
The component parsing 一 + 丨 and the ‘cutting across a line’ interpretation are part of one disputed analysis; no independent semantic role for each stroke is established.
The Shijing transcription provides transmitted text, not a dated physical witness. Exact dating of the poem’s composition and earliest surviving written attestation of 七 remain unverified here.

The official GetUnihanData record was attempted twice and inaccessible, and the official code-chart PDF fetch exceeded the tool’s content limit. Local kMandarin qī was checked, but its requested official click-through page could not be verified. No other proposed component requires a component-specific sound comparison for this entry.

No need for a local corpus extract is established: the inspected references are character-specific or scholarly and this research does not rely on repeated bulk material; reuse permissions for any bulk extract were not established.
The earliest graphic referent and spoken name of 七 are not independently established. The cut interpretation remains disputed against the account of numeral use from oracle-bone writing onward.

The proposed whole-graph loan from a word meaning ‘cut’ is not proven by a matched 七–切 pronunciation comparison in a single reconstruction system. No independently established name or pronunciation for a depicted cutting object was found; the loan claim therefore remains uncertain.
The claimed 一 + 丨 semantic analysis belongs to the disputed cut-origin account. No separate semantic role for either stroke is independently established.
The transmitted Shijing text is not a dated physical witness; the poem’s composition date and earliest surviving written use of 七 were not independently verified in this pass.

The official Unicode Unihan character endpoint was inaccessible. The local kMandarin row qī and local Baxter–Sagart row for 七 (MC tshit, OC *[tsʰ]i[t]) were checked in the input but are not external evidence. No component sound role is asserted.

The selected Commons images are modern SVG redrawings of script styles, not artifact photographs. The exact original SVG link is exposed from the verified description page, but its sharded upload URL could not be copied through the web tool; image candidates remain limited to pages with verified identity and license.
